overview: This entry represents the Free City of Danzig, a Baltic port and surrounding territory created in 1920 under League of Nations protection, with special Polish rights. Most inhabitants were German-speaking; Polish and Jewish communities also shaped local life. Its actual history ran from 1920 to 1939, beyond the map’s shorter 1930 to 1938 display interval. This is today’s Gdańsk, but the card concerns that particular interwar political arrangement.

periods.title: The interwar Free City
periods.summary: A separate government operated under League of Nations protection and treaty arrangements with Poland.

periods.title: Nazi domination and annexation
periods.summary: The Nazi electoral victory was followed by repression and, in 1939, German annexation.

sections.title: A port with an unusual government

items.text: The city had its own Senate and parliament, the Volkstag. Poland represented it abroad, while the territory belonged to Poland’s customs area and Poland had rights to use its port. A joint harbor board managed important port affairs. Everyday trade therefore depended on cooperation between institutions with different national loyalties.

Writing sample: Article 3 of the constitution published in 1922 reads, “Die Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus.” It means, “State authority comes from the people.” This short German sentence is preserved in a modern transcription of the published constitution. Later repression makes the promise especially striking.

The constitution gave male and female citizens over twenty the right to elect representatives, subject to stated legal exclusions, and declared equal civic rights for women and men. These were promises written into law. Reading them alongside the later persecution shows why a constitution’s words and a government’s behavior need separate examination.

The Free City had separate postal services connected with its German and Polish institutions. The surviving equipment, papers and photographs in the Polish Post Office museum make this unusual arrangement tangible. Mailing a letter involved offices and routes that also carried political significance in a city with competing national claims.

The Polish Gymnasium began classes on 9 May 1922 in former barracks. In its first school year it had 199 pupils and ten teachers. Some children were not fluent in Polish, so language teaching received particular attention. A school could be a place to strengthen a family’s cultural ties as well as learn ordinary subjects.

School costs affected children’s choices. The Polish Gymnasium charged twenty Danzig gulden a month, and the city’s historical account explains that many pupils moved into Polish commercial schools instead of completing the gymnasium course. Academic schooling was not simply a matter of turning up with a notebook; a family had to afford the fees.

Gedania, founded in September 1922, organized several sports for women and men. Its prewar membership reached about 550, mainly Poles, but also included Jews and Germans until the mid-1930s. Rowing and yacht clubs also appeared in 1922. The waterfront offered people exercise and friendships as well as work.

sections.title: A working family and small traces of daily life

items.text: Franciszek Szmelter leased the railway station’s round-the-clock restaurant in 1933. His wife Maria, who came from a Jewish family in Mostar, helped manage the business and kept its accounts. Museum collections preserve family photographs and restaurant cutlery marked with their surname, linking a large transport hub to one household’s work.

Maria also ran the Polish Station Mission, helping people find jobs and somewhere to live and offering overnight rooms at the station. Railway and school employees sometimes earned extra money in the restaurant after their regular work. The family’s business was therefore also part of a network of practical help and supplementary income.

Small printed papers reveal habits that official ceremonies miss. The Polish Academy of Sciences Library preserves interwar advertising labels, photographs and slips confirming confession, which allowed their holders to receive Easter communion. Such religious paperwork records one community’s practice; the Free City’s residents did not all share the same faith.
The Nazi Party won an absolute majority in the Volkstag election of 28 May 1933. Political power increasingly served Nazi aims.

The Great Synagogue, which had survived the violence of November 1938, was sold to the city under Nazi domination and demolished in May 1939. A major community landmark disappeared before the war began.

Photographs from 1935 show antisemitic markings on Jewish-owned businesses. A 1939 image records another Jewish shop forced to close. These are concrete traces of persecution in ordinary shopping streets: it changed where families could work and whether their neighbors were allowed to participate safely in city life.

ending.text: On 1 September 1939, Nazi Germany attacked Polish installations and annexed the Free City. The political arrangement ended amid war and repression. After the war, the city became part of Poland; much of its German population fled or was expelled. Modern Gdańsk continued with a profoundly changed population.
